summary:
Project HeatWatch is a free, public web dashboard that identifies haze-prone fire hotspots across Malaysia and shows when the risk is highest. We harmonised NASA MODIS and VIIRS fire detections into one consistent record from 2000 to 2026, using per-cell calibration that achieved a median monthly error of 13.1% against actual VIIRS observations. On top of this, a Holt-Winters model forecasts typical seasonal burning, and a haze model combines Indonesian fire heat from Sumatra and Kalimantan, NASA POWER wind and rainfall, and El Niño conditions into a Low, Moderate or Severe risk level, tuned with MERRA-2 aerosol data.

This addresses the challenge directly. Existing regional systems detect hotspots, but few assess whether fires will become haze in Malaysia. HeatWatch fills that gap with a burning calendar, area and date comparison, timelapse, and CSV and report downloads.

It matters because Malaysia is repeatedly affected by transboundary haze. Government agencies, agriculture and tourism operators, and the public can plan ahead using open data and simple, explainable methods.
details:
Project HeatWatch is a free web dashboard that shows which parts of Malaysia are at risk of fire hotspots and haze, and when. Malaysia is repeatedly affected by transboundary haze from fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan. Existing regional systems such as the ASEAN ASMC detect hotspots, but few judge whether those fires are likely to become haze in Malaysia. HeatWatch is built to fill that gap.
How it works
We take NASA FIRMS fire detections from MODIS (Terra and Aqua, 2000 onward) and VIIRS (2012 onward), then clean them by keeping vegetation fires only and removing low-confidence detections and duplicates.
MODIS and VIIRS see fires at different resolutions, so raw data shows an artificial jump in 2012. We convert MODIS counts into VIIRS-equivalent units using per-cell ratios on a 25 km grid, calibrated on the 2012-2020 overlap. This gives one consistent hotspot record from 2000 to 2026. Monthly counts correlate at r = 0.98 across the overlap, and on held-out months (2019-2020) the method had a median monthly error of 13.1%. It beat Poisson regression, random forest and gradient boosting.
A Holt-Winters model forecasts typical seasonal burning activity 24 months ahead, with an uncertainty band.
A haze model combines Indonesian fire heat (Sumatra and Kalimantan), NASA POWER wind and rainfall, El Niño conditions and Malaysian readings into a Low / Moderate / Severe risk level. NASA MERRA-2 aerosol data was used to tune and check it.
What users can do
The web app offers a monthly burning calendar, area and radius search, date-range comparison (A vs B), a timelapse, and CSV and report downloads. It is live on a public link and needs no installation.
Benefits and intended impact
Government agencies can plan around expected burning seasons.
Agriculture and tourism operators can adjust schedules ahead of likely haze periods.
The public can see risk in a simple, accessible form.
It runs entirely on free, open NASA data with simple, explainable methods, so it is cheap to maintain and easy for policy makers to trust.
Tools and technologies
Python (NumPy, Matplotlib), Google Colab, NASA FIRMS/EarthData (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS S-NPP 375 m), NASA POWER, NASA MERRA-2, Holt-Winters forecasting, HTML/CSS for the dashboard, and Vercel for hosting. Claude was used for code optimisation and layout formatting.
What makes it creative
It targets haze risk specifically, rather than only reporting hotspots.
It links Indonesian fires, wind direction and rainfall to Malaysian outcomes.
It chose a transparent calibration method over complex machine learning, after testing the alternatives, so that results are explainable.
Factors we considered
Sensor differences between MODIS and VIIRS, and the limited Terra-only record from 2000 to mid-2002.
A hotspot is a thermal detection, not burned area or smoke volume.
Holt-Winters shows typical seasonality and will not predict extreme years such as 2015 and 2019, so extreme events are flagged by the haze model instead.
The haze thresholds need further testing against independent air-quality records and future seasons.
